background.definition: Lymphedema is a chronic swelling arising from the abnormal accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid due to primary or secondary alterations of the lymphatic flow.

list.listitem: A 1.33 per 1000 prevalence of chronic edema from different causes has been reported in the United States.

Congenital: developmental abnormalities of the lymphatic system (primary lymphedema), either evident at birth (congenital lymphedema) or not (lymphedema praecox and lymphedema tarda). Primary lymphedema from developmental abnormalities of the lymphatic system is uncommon; cases already evident at birth (congenital lymphedema) or developing after age 35 years (lymphedema tarda) are exceedingly rare. In some patients with positive family history, causative heritable genetic mutations have been identified (FLT4 gene for Milroy's disease, FOXC2 gene for a subset of patients with lymphedema praecox).

Morbid obesity is an increasingly common cause of lymphedema, although it must be distinguished from lipedema. It also contributes to lymphedema primarily caused by other conditions such as malignancy or after lymph node dissection.

Filariasis: lymph nodal parasitic infestation by W. bancrofti (widely diffuse in tropical areas) or B. malayi (in India, China, and other Southeast Asian areas). Most common cause worldwide of secondary lymphedema.

Podoconiosis: a geochemical disease induced by the absorption of ultrafine silica particles from the soil through the skin of the feet in susceptible individuals, leading to a progressive obliterative endolymphangitis. Has 5.5% prevalence in some tropical areas.
Iatrogenic: impaired lymphatic drainage after surgical removal or irradiation of lymph nodes. More than 1 in 5 women will develop unilateral arm lymphedema after surgery for breast cancer.

Tumor invasion from neoplastic disorders, including Kaposi’s sarcoma. Secondary cancer-related lymphedema has been observed in more than 80% of newly assessed patients attending lymphedema treatment clinics in the United Kingdom.
Other possible acquired conditions, such as infections, insect bites, burns, traumas, and complications from peripheral vascular surgery.

An imbalance of the lymphatic flow causes the normal volume of interstitial fluid formation to exceed the rate of lymphatic return, with the consequent stagnation of high-molecular-weight proteins and an increased oncotic pressure in the interstitium.
Fluid collection in the extravascular space results in local swelling, and is followed by a chronic inflammatory reaction, which causes extensive irreversible fibrosclerotic changes.

The hardening and thickening of soft tissues causes further damage and congestion of the remaining outflow lymphatics. This may lead to fissuration and lymph leakage, with frequent secondary infections.
An increase in limb circumference with pitting or nonpitting edema is a typical clinical feature. C
Routine laboratory investigations may help rule out systemic disease. C
Lymphoscintigraphy is currently the gold standard for imaging studies; echocardiography, Doppler ultrasonography, CT, MRI, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, and PET may be useful in selected cases. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Peripheral edema from congestive heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, superior vena cava syndrome, and hepatic or renal insufficiency

Differential.Differential_Features: Leg varicosities and brown hemosiderin deposits often present, improves overnight
Usually acute, of less than 72 hours’ duration, unilateral, painful
Typically sparing the dorsum of the foot

Differential.Differential_Name: Limb enlargement related to major obesity
Differential.Differential_Features: Symmetric, soft, bilateral large limbs in overweight patients
History of calcium channel blockers, NSAIDS, prednisone, or other drugs that cause edema

list.listitem: Three grades or stages of lymphedema:
Grade I: Pitting edema that reduces with limb elevation
Grade II: Nonpitting edema that does not reduce with limb elevation
Grade III: Lymphostatic elephantiasis with trophic skin changes

Patients typically present with limb enlargement, pitting of tissues, and increased thickness of skin folds in early stages. They may have various degrees of nonpitting edema in longstanding forms. Typically, the dorsal skin at the base of the second toe cannot be pinched (positive Kaposi-Stemmer sign). Orange peel and warty skin texture, with browny induration, reminiscent of elephant skin, may be observed in advanced stages.

Persistent edema for longer than 3 months is more likely to be lymphedema. A volume of greater than 200 mL as measured by water displacement or a 5% or greater than 1 cm increase in arm circumference have been indicated as reliable indicators of arm lymphedema. However, no univocal objective criteria used by all investigators have been established so far. Moreover, in the clinical setting, reliance on these indicators has shown many pitfalls.
Gynecological lymphedema may be difficult to recognize. Its symptoms, besides genital swelling, labial thickening, and changes in skin texture and pubic hair growth, also include lymphorrhea.
It is important to rule out other systemic causes of edema such as renal disease or heart failure.
Sudden onset, rapid progression, and/or associated pain should always prompt the suspicion of a malignancy, including lymphangiosarcoma.
Consider filariasis in residents of tropical areas where that disease is endemic.

Disease severity and progression can be assessed using sequential circumferential limb measurements and water displacement volumetry. More recently, other noninvasive techniques have been proposed, including bioelectric impedance analysis, tonometry, and perometry.
Routine initial evaluation should include complete blood cell count, urinalysis, electrolytes, blood sugar, thyroid hormones, and albumin to rule out systemic disease.

Imaging studies should be ordered if indicated by the history or physical examination. They include echocardiography, to rule out pulmonary hypertension and congestive heart failure; Doppler ultrasonography to rule out deep venous thrombosis and venous insufficiency; lymphoscintigraphy to assess residual lymphatic function or provide information for treatment planning; and CT or MRI, which may show a distinctive honeycomb pattern of the subcutaneous tissues if lymphedema is present and may also detect malignant tumors with lymph nodal involvement. Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI and PET may also be useful for lymph node assessment. Near infrared fluorescent imaging with indocyanine green is another emerging technique.
Histopathologic examination should be performed to rule out underlying malignancy in patients with radionuclide findings suggestive of secondary lymphedema with no obvious etiology.
Instruct patients to avoid any trauma and limb constriction from tight clothing, and to perform regular cleaning to prevent superinfection. B

Recommend early conservative management with regular individual physical exercise, manual lymphatic drainage, the use of compression bandages and garments, and of static gradient or intermittent pneumatic pump compression devices. B

Prescribe antiparasitic treatment in case of filariasis, and topical or systemic antibiotic and/or antifungal treatments if cellulitis ensues. A single dose of ivermectin + diethylcarbamazine + albendazole is recommended for lymphatic filariasis; however, antiparasitic treatment has not been shown to prevent lymphangitic flares in patients with lymphedema.B
Consider surgery if severe lymphedema impairs normal routine daily activities or prevents successful conservative management. C

Adjuvant treatments useful to boost clearing of accumulated interstitial proteins include benzopyrones, flavonoids, and coumarin. Their efficacy and safety, however, still deserve further rigorous assessment.
Treatment with antiparasitic drugs should be prescribed in case of filariasis. Diethylcarbamazine plus ivermectin has been found to be an effective combination treatment against microfilariasis.

However, a randomized trial in patients with lymphatic filariasis compared a single dose of ivermectin + diethylcarbamazine + albendazole with a single dose of diethylcarbamazine + albendazole with a single dose of the two drug regimen once yearly for three years. The three drug regimen was superior to a single dose of the two drug regimen, and non-inferior to the two drug regimen given annually.

Surgery is rarely indicated as the primary treatment modality and does not obviate the need for long-term conservative management. It should be considered when severe lymphedema unresponsive to conservative therapy impairs normal routine daily activities or prevents successful conservative management.

Surgical procedures include techniques aimed to improve lymphatic circulation by creating new routes for lymph drainage (lymphangioplasty, lympholymphatic or lymphovenous anastomoses, lymph node transfer and lymphatic grafting), more suitable on patients with early lymphedema, and the removal of redundant subcutaneous tissue by staged or radical excision techniques or liposuction. A possible worsening of lymphatic impairment with these last procedures, which do not correct the underlying vascular defect, should be taken into account.
Recommend regular physical exercise, initiated by well-trained therapists, to improve lymph flow and venous return through repeated muscle activity.

Although the literature contains no evidence to suggest the most effective treatment, a common recommendation is early conservative management intended to prevent irreversible fibrosis by redirecting the accumulated lymph to neighboring regions with still functioning lymphatics.

This includes manual lymphatic drainage, the use of compression bandages and garments, static gradient compression devices, and intermittent pneumatic pump compression. The use of these last devices is contraindicated in case of active infection, deep vein thrombosis, and congestive heart failure.

Instruct patients to elevate the affected extremity when at rest, especially at night, and to promptly wear customized elastic and graduated compression garments just before standing upright. These should be worn daily and removed at bedtime.
Instruct patients to avoid tight clothing and jewelry, to maintain good hygiene and avoid trauma or extreme heat or cold, and to contact their physician at the first signs of infection.
Regular cleaning and the use of topical moisturizers may help to remove scales and keep the skin soft, avoiding fissuration.
Hospitalization may be required if severe complications (cellulitis or sepsis) occur.
It is also necessary for surgical treatment and, subsequently, during initial postoperative follow-up.
Cellulitis and deep vein thrombosis are complications discussed in other chapters.
Recurrent bacterial lymphangitis may be managed with long-term prophylactic antibiotic treatment.
Malignant degeneration (lymphangiosarcoma) is aggressively managed with surgical amputation of the affected limb.

Lymphangiosarcoma may occur in up to 10% of patients with longstanding lymphedema. It has a poor prognosis (<10% 5-year survival), and it is most commonly observed in postmastectomy lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome). B
Risk factors for lymphedema in breast cancer survivors include mastectomy rather than lumpectomy, axillary dissection, radiation therapy, and positive axillary nodes.B
